```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 120)
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

## Overview

`BamScaleR` is a multithreaded BAM reader, built on the `ompBAM` OpenMP engine, that
returns the same native Bioconductor objects as the standard readers, so it can
take the place of `Rsamtools::scanBam` and `GenomicAlignments::readGAlignments`
in existing analyses (see `?bam_read` for the differences).

Reading a BAM is only one step of an analysis, so a faster reader speeds a workflow
end-to-end **only in proportion to the time that workflow spends reading**
(Amdahl's law). This vignette summarises benchmarks that quantify *both* the raw
read speedup and its end-to-end effect on two standard workflows — coverage/bigWig
track generation and ATAC-seq fragment-size QC — with BamScaleR output verified
**identical** to that of the standard tools.

```{r load-data}
## Benchmark summary tables shipped with the package (see "Data provenance").
extdata <- function(f) {
  system.file("extdata", f, package = "BamScaleR", mustWork = TRUE)
}
bench    <- read.csv(extdata("benchmark_summary.csv"))
manifest <- read.csv(extdata("benchmark_encode_manifest.csv"))
checks   <- read.csv(extdata("benchmark_correctness.csv"))
run_info <- read.csv(extdata("benchmark_run_info.csv"))
info     <- setNames(run_info$value, run_info$field)
```

```{r results-data}
fx  <- function(x, digits = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "fx"), x)
rng <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f--%.1f", min(x), max(x))
big <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)

is_bs   <- function(d) d$method_family == "BamScaleR"
fastest <- function(d) d[which.min(d$median_s), , drop = FALSE]

## Read patterns (single file, "fair" track): the single-threaded standard
## reader vs BamScaleR's fastest configuration over the thread sweep.
rd <- bench[bench$benchmark == "read", ]
read_labels <- c(step1 = "Core fields", galignments = "GAlignments",
                 seqqual = "Sequence + quality")
read_fields <- c(step1 = "qname/flag/rname/pos/mapq/cigar",
                 galignments = "-> GAlignments object",
                 seqqual = "seq + base quality")
read_tbl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(read_labels), function(wl) {
  x   <- rd[rd$workload == wl, ]
  bs  <- fastest(x[is_bs(x), ])
  std <- fastest(x[!is_bs(x), ])
  data.frame(Workload = read_labels[[wl]], Reads = read_fields[[wl]],
             `Standard (s)` = round(std$median_s, 1),
             `BamScaleR (s)` = round(bs$median_s, 1),
             Threads = bs$threads, Speedup = std$median_s / bs$median_s,
             check.names = FALSE)
}))

## Thread scaling: the one-thread comparison with the standard reader, and
## BamScaleR's own speedup from 1 to 48 threads and beyond 24 threads.
bs_at <- function(n) vapply(names(read_labels), function(wl)
  rd$median_s[rd$workload == wl & is_bs(rd) & rd$threads == n], numeric(1))
std_s <- vapply(names(read_labels), function(wl)
  rd$median_s[rd$workload == wl & !is_bs(rd)], numeric(1))
best_bs <- vapply(names(read_labels), function(wl)
  min(rd$median_s[rd$workload == wl & is_bs(rd)]), numeric(1))
speedup_1t    <- std_s / bs_at(1)
scaling_48    <- bs_at(1) / bs_at(48)
gain_after_24 <- bs_at(24) / best_bs

## Workflows (single file): each arm's configuration with the lowest median
## end-to-end time. An endpoint's time is the sum of its phase medians, and its
## read fraction is the standard pipeline's read share of that sum.
wf <- bench[bench$benchmark == "workflow" & bench$scenario == "single", ]
wf_best <- function(wl) {
  x <- wf[wf$workload == wl, ]
  list(bs = fastest(x[is_bs(x), ]), std = fastest(x[!is_bs(x), ]))
}
wf_endpoint <- function(wl, endpoint, with_write) {
  b <- wf_best(wl)
  phases <- function(r) {
    r$read_s + r$compute_s + if (with_write) r$write_s else 0
  }
  data.frame(Endpoint = endpoint, Layer = "workflow",
             `Read fraction` = b$std$read_s / phases(b$std),
             Speedup = phases(b$std) / phases(b$bs), check.names = FALSE)
}
spectrum_tbl <- rbind(
  data.frame(Endpoint = paste(read_tbl$Workload, "(read)"), Layer = "read",
             `Read fraction` = 1, Speedup = read_tbl$Speedup,
             check.names = FALSE),
  wf_endpoint("coverage", "Coverage -> RleList", with_write = FALSE),
  wf_endpoint("coverage", "Coverage -> bigWig", with_write = TRUE),
  wf_endpoint("atacqc", "ATAC fragment-size QC", with_write = TRUE)
)
spectrum_tbl <- spectrum_tbl[order(-spectrum_tbl$Speedup), ]
rownames(spectrum_tbl) <- NULL
endpoint_speedup <- setNames(spectrum_tbl$Speedup, spectrum_tbl$Endpoint)
cov_best <- wf_best("coverage")
cov_read_speedup <- cov_best$std$read_s / cov_best$bs$read_s

## Multi-file matched cores: standard / BamScaleR median, same cores per arm.
mc <- bench[bench$comparison_track == "matched-cores", ]
matched <- vapply(c(coverage = "coverage", atacqc = "atacqc"), function(wl) {
  x <- mc[mc$workload == wl, ]
  x$median_s[!is_bs(x)] / x$median_s[is_bs(x)]
}, numeric(1))

## Run description
single_bam <- manifest[manifest$role == "single", ]
n_aln  <- unique(rd$n_records)
n_iter <- unique(bench$iterations[bench$scenario == "single"])
cpu    <- gsub("\\((R|TM)\\)", "", info[["cpu_model"]])  # Intel(R) Xeon(R) ...
cpu    <- trimws(sub(" CPU @.*$", "", cpu))
anchor_n <- checks$n_compared[checks$check == "atacseqqc_anchor"]
stopifnot(length(n_aln) == 1L, length(n_iter) == 1L, length(anchor_n) == 1L)
```

The numbers below are a concise summary of a representative benchmark run
(a deeply sequenced public ENCODE ATAC-seq BAM, `r single_bam$accession`,
`r big(n_aln)` alignments; `r cpu`, `r info[["logical_cores"]]` logical cores;
warm page cache; median of `r n_iter` iterations). They are computed, when this
vignette is built, from summary tables shipped with the package (see
[Data provenance](#data-provenance)). The
benchmark harness that produces them is in `inst/benchmarks/`
(`run_server_benchmark.R`, `run_workflow_benchmark.R`); see the last section to
reproduce the full results.

## Read throughput on a single large BAM

On a single large BAM, BamScaleR reads **`r rng(read_tbl$Speedup)`x faster**
than the standard reader across three representative access patterns, because it
spreads the BGZF decode across cores and assembles the output objects in native
code:

```{r read-table}
knitr::kable(
  transform(read_tbl, Speedup = sprintf("%.2fx", Speedup)),
  caption = paste0("Single-file read throughput: best BamScaleR configuration ",
                   "vs the single-threaded standard reader (median of ",
                   n_iter, " iterations).")
)
```

```{r read-plot, eval=has_ggplot}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(read_tbl, aes(stats::reorder(Workload, Speedup), Speedup)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a78d6", width = 0.65) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2fx", Speedup)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "speedup over standard reader (dashed = parity)",
       title = "Single-file read speedup") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

Two points. At **one thread** BamScaleR is `r rng(speedup_1t)`x as fast
as the single-threaded readers (from native-code object assembly); most of the
win comes from threading, and the scaling is **strongly sublinear**: going from 1
to 48 threads speeds BamScaleR itself up by `r rng(scaling_48)`x, and no thread
count beyond 24 is more than
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (max(gain_after_24) - 1))` faster than 24 threads. The
value is not near-linear scaling but the ability to use cores that a
single-threaded reader cannot use at all -- as on one large BAM in an interactive
session. Object-free command-line decoders such as `samtools` reach several-fold
higher *raw* throughput, but return no Bioconductor object; BamScaleR's role is
fast, object-faithful decoding *inside* R.

## End-to-end impact tracks the read fraction

Embedding BamScaleR as the read step of a complete workflow, the end-to-end speedup
follows how read-dominated that workflow is (Amdahl's law):

```{r spectrum-table}
knitr::kable(
  transform(spectrum_tbl,
            `Read fraction` = paste0(round(100 * spectrum_tbl$`Read fraction`), "%"),
            Speedup = sprintf("%.2fx", Speedup)),
  caption = "End-to-end speedup by workload endpoint. Read-pattern rows are single-file read throughput; workflow rows are end-to-end. Read fraction is the share of the standard pipeline spent reading."
)
```

```{r spectrum-plot, eval=has_ggplot, fig.height=4.4}
ggplot(spectrum_tbl, aes(stats::reorder(Endpoint, Speedup), Speedup, fill = `Read fraction`)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2fx", Speedup)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.4) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#cfe0f3", high = "#12355b", labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "end-to-end speedup (dashed = parity)", fill = "read\nfraction",
       title = "The gain tracks the read fraction") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

- **ATAC fragment-size QC** is nearly pure read, so BamScaleR's read speedup carries
  through almost intact:
  **`r fx(endpoint_speedup[["ATAC fragment-size QC"]])`** end-to-end.
- **Coverage -> bigWig** is dominated by the shared, single-threaded
  `rtracklayer::export.bw` step (identical work on both arms), so the end-to-end
  gain is bounded at **`r fx(endpoint_speedup[["Coverage -> bigWig"]])`** even
  though the read phase itself is `r fx(cov_read_speedup, 1)` faster.
  Stopping at the in-memory coverage `RleList` -- what many analyses consume
  next -- recovers a **`r fx(endpoint_speedup[["Coverage -> RleList"]])`** gain.
  (`bam_coverage()` and `bam_coverage_bigwig()` compute these endpoints directly
  inside the reader, removing the R-side read phase entirely; see the function
  documentation.)

## A note on cores and fairness

A multithreaded reader can occupy cores a single-threaded one cannot. At **matched
core counts** (both arms given the same number of cores) the two readers are
within about 20% of each other for multi-file processing
(coverage ~`r fx(matched[["coverage"]])`, ATAC ~`r fx(matched[["atacqc"]])`):
the single-threaded reader already saturates a machine by parallelising *across*
files, so BamScaleR's multi-file advantage comes specifically from also threading
*within* a file -- which pays off when there are fewer files than cores.

## Beyond reading: in-reader aggregation

For workflows whose endpoint is a summary rather than the alignments themselves,
BamScaleR provides four functions that fold the computation inside the
multithreaded reader, so no per-read R objects are ever materialised:
`fragment_sizes()` (paired-end fragment-size distribution),
`mapq_dist()` (mapping-quality distribution), `bam_coverage()` (per-base coverage
`RleList`), and `bam_coverage_bigwig()` (single-pass BAM to bigWig with parallel
block compression). The first three are tested `identical()` to
`table(abs(scanBam(isize)))`, `table(scanBam(mapq))` and
`coverage(readGAlignments())`; the bigWig, read back with `rtracklayer`, has
the same values as `bam_coverage()`, and its parallel compression gives a file
byte-identical to the package's own serial writer. These remove the R-side read
phase from the Amdahl decomposition above; their benchmarks are not part of the
data shipped with this vignette.

## Output is identical to the standard tools

Before the timings, the outputs were checked against the standard tools. On the
full files, at one thread, the
coverage `RleList` was `identical()` to `GenomicAlignments::coverage()` on
`readGAlignments` output, and the ATAC fragment-size table was `identical()` to
the one from `Rsamtools::scanBam` and to `ATACseqQC::fragSizeDist` over all
`r big(anchor_n)` alignments; the read-pattern outputs were checked on a 1-kb
window (`benchmark_correctness.csv`). The package's unit
tests compare coverage with `coverage(readGAlignments())` and the fragment-size
and MAPQ tables with `scanBam()` on the example BAM at 1, 2 and 4 threads.

## Try it

```{r demo, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
library(BamScaleR)
bam <- ompBAM::example_BAM("Unsorted")

## Alignment fields as a GAlignments object (as from readGAlignments)
ga <- bam_read(bam, what = c("rname", "pos", "cigar", "strand"),
               as = "GAlignments", threads = 2)
ga

## ...or core fields as a data.frame; `threads` controls within-file parallelism
df <- bam_read(bam, what = c("qname", "flag", "mapq"),
               as = "data.frame", threads = 2)
head(df)
```

## Data provenance

Every result in this vignette is computed, when the vignette is
built, from four small CSV files shipped with the package in `inst/extdata/`:

```{r load-data-shown, ref.label="load-data", echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
```

- `benchmark_summary.csv`: one row per benchmarked configuration
  (`r nrow(bench)` rows): median wall-clock time and, for the single-file
  workflows, the median read, compute and write phases.
- `benchmark_encode_manifest.csv`: the `r nrow(manifest)` public ENCODE
  ATAC-seq alignment BAMs (accession, experiment, biosample, size, md5 checksum,
  read count and download URL).
- `benchmark_run_info.csv`: host, software versions and git commit of the run.
- `benchmark_correctness.csv`: the output-equivalence checks the timings were
  gated on.

They are a subset of the result tables of benchmark run `r info[["run_id"]]`
(started `r info[["run_date"]]`; BamScaleR `r info[["bamscaler_version"]]` at
git commit `r substr(info[["git_head"]], 1, 7)`; R `r info[["r_version"]]`;
`r cpu`, `r info[["logical_cores"]]` logical cores), produced by the harness in
`inst/benchmarks/` and reduced to these files by
`inst/scripts/make_benchmark_extdata.R`. The header of that script records the
exact command line of every step: corpus selection from the ENCODE portal
(`select_encode_atac.R`), md5-verified download (`download_atac_data.R`), the
read-pattern and workflow benchmarks (`run_server_benchmark.R`,
`run_workflow_benchmark.R`), and merging of the staged runs (`merge_runs.R`).

The summary numbers are derived as follows:

- **Read patterns** compare the single-threaded standard reader with
  BamScaleR's fastest configuration over a sweep of
  `r paste(sort(unique(rd$threads[is_bs(rd)])), collapse = ", ")` OpenMP
  threads, on the same file, both returning the same object.
- **Workflows** take, for each arm, the configuration with the lowest median
  end-to-end time. An endpoint's time is the sum of its median phases (read +
  compute, plus the track write for the bigWig endpoint), and its read fraction
  is the standard pipeline's read time divided by that sum.
- **Matched cores** divide the standard arm's median time by BamScaleR's on the
  `r unique(mc$n_files)`-file cohort, with both arms running one thread per file
  on the same number of cores.

```{r manifest-table}
encode_page <- sub("@@download/.*$", "", manifest$url)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Role       = manifest$role,
    Accession  = sprintf("[%s](%s)", manifest$accession, encode_page),
    Experiment = manifest$experiment,
    Biosample  = manifest$biosample,
    `Reads (M)` = round(manifest$total_reads / 1e6, 1),
    `Size (GB)` = round(manifest$file_size_bytes / 1e9, 2),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  caption = paste0(
    "The ", nrow(manifest), " public ENCODE ATAC-seq alignment BAMs (GRCh38, ",
    "paired-end) benchmarked. The single file is the target of every ",
    "single-file benchmark; the ", sum(manifest$role == "multi"),
    " multi files form the cohort of the matched-cores comparison. Read ",
    "counts are the ENCODE QC total reads; md5 checksums and download URLs ",
    "are in ",
    "benchmark_encode_manifest.csv.")
)
```

## Reproducing the full benchmarks

The complete benchmark harness ships under `inst/benchmarks/`; its `README.md`
lists the additional packages and command-line tools it needs.

```{r repro, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
dir(system.file("benchmarks", package = "BamScaleR"))
# select_encode_atac.R        : select the ATAC-seq corpus from the ENCODE portal
# download_atac_data.R        : fetch, md5-verify and index the selected BAMs
# run_server_benchmark.R      : read-pattern micro-benchmarks (step1 / GAlignments / seq+qual)
# run_workflow_benchmark.R    : end-to-end coverage and ATAC fragment-size QC workflows
# merge_runs.R                : merge staged runs into one result directory

## Reduce a finished run to the CSVs this vignette reads
system.file("scripts", "make_benchmark_extdata.R", package = "BamScaleR")
```

Each benchmark writes machine-readable result tables (`summary.csv`) plus host
and correctness metadata; `make_benchmark_extdata.R` extracts from them the
files in `inst/extdata/` from which the summary figures above are derived.
